newsitem.title: USA: Fears of wage inflation weigh on U.S. Treasuries.
newsitem.headline: Fears of wage inflation weigh on U.S. Treasuries.

text.p: Fears of growing wage pressures drove bond prices lower on Friday as traders began to price in another tightening of monetary policy in May.
The Labor Department reported that 175,000 nonfarm payroll jobs were created in March, below consensus estimates of 196,000.

But, as some economists predicted, the overall number was not the main focus, playing second fiddle to the wage components of the report. The March report contained the largest average hourly earnings gain in seven years and the highest overtime levels in 41 years, economists said.

Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan has spoken repeatedly of the dangers of wage inflation and this report was seen as confirming his hunch that wage inflation was bound to occur and make another tightening of monetary policy more likely at the Fed's next policy-making meeting on May 20.
"Hours worked were very high (34.8). We saw a big jump last month and everyone expected a big pullback, but we didn't get it," said Christopher Low, senior economist at HSBC Markets Inc.

Low said even if one did not believe the increase seen in average hourly earnings led directly to inflation, the fact was that consumers were earning more, working more and inevitably would spend more. And consumer spending levels already were high.

Further depressing market sentiment was the expectation that another very strong overall report -- in excess of 200,000 new jobs -- loomed in April as seasonal factors would inflate the number. That will be the last payrolls number seen by Federal Open Market Committee members before they meet again.
"Stocks had just finished pricing in another move in May," said Low. "All in all this was not a very encouraging report."
Elliott Platt, director of economic research at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp, said it was important not to dwell on individual monthly totals.

"The fact that this number was below consensus doesn't make it a good number. Even at 175,000 you have more payroll growth than is consistent with a GDP growth rate of 2.0 percent," Platt said. "It's still a very, very strong number."
Platt said very high levels in manufacturing hours (42.1), overtime and a lower unemployment rate (5.2 percent) all summed up to accelerating inflation and a further 25-basis-point tightening in May.

Doug Schindewolf, money market economist at Smith Barney Inc, added that while the overall number was below expectations, other components were quite strong. Fed policymakers have expressed concern on unemployment levels and another 0.1 percent drop would have to worry them, he said.

"It certainly didn't take the threat of a followup tightening off the radar screen," Schindewolf said. "The upward creep in average hourly earnings continued and the work week overall -- but especially in manufacturing -- was very high."
Schindewolf said an upward ratcheting of interest rates by 25 basis points was likely in May and chances were 50-50 another would occur in July.
"At some point they have to take a pause, probably after the second or third tightening. But the pause won't happen now," Schindewolf said.
Treasuries swooned following the report with the yield on the long bond lingering at around 7.12 percent in the late morning, its highest level in roughly seven months.
